slides.title: Pages organize storage; objects organize meaning
keyPoints: One page can contain many C++ objects
One object can span many pages
Page permissions do not establish object bounds
slides.narration: A page is a fixed-size region of virtual address space. A C++ object is a language-level value with a type, lifetime, and bounds. These units need not line up. A large vector can span several pages, and a single page can hold several unrelated allocations. This matters when discussing safety: a hardware check may permit an address even though it lies beyond the array you are allowed to access. Conversely, crossing a page boundary is normal when the allocation and mappings cover both pages. We will use tiny page sizes in arithmetic demonstrations so every boundary is visible without pretending those sizes describe actual hardware.
actions: Predict the result and name the mapping or invariant that supports it before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: Does crossing a page boundary necessarily mean an array access is invalid?
question.answer: No. The array may span multiple valid mapped pages; object bounds and page boundaries are different.

slides.title: A three-byte span can need two mappings
keyPoints: Model page size is eight bytes
The offset wraps at a page boundary
The next page may use a distant frame
slides.narration: The modeled span begins at virtual address seven and covers three bytes. With eight-byte pages, seven is page zero at offset seven. Eight is page one at offset zero, and nine is page one at offset one. We map page zero to frame three and page one to frame nine, producing physical addresses thirty-one, seventy-two, and seventy-three. The large jump comes from the frame mapping, not from skipped virtual bytes. These are integer calculations in an explicit model, not accesses to real physical memory. The output shows why checking only the first byte of a multi-byte operation cannot establish permissions for the whole span.

slides.title: A frame is the physical partner of a page
keyPoints: Virtual page number selects a mapping
Frame number selects backing storage
Translation preserves the offset
slides.narration: If page five maps to frame two, the number five does not become part of the offset. The mapping replaces the page-number portion while retaining the byte’s position within the page. For a frame size of four thousand ninety-six bytes, frame two begins at eight thousand one hundred ninety-two. Adding offset nine gives eight thousand two hundred one. Adjacent virtual pages can select distant frames while still presenting a contiguous virtual array. That flexibility supports allocation and isolation. A device that requires physically contiguous storage needs a stronger platform mechanism; an ordinary contiguous C++ container only promises contiguity in its own address space.

question.prompt: What does a contiguous vector fail to promise about its backing frames?
question.answer: It does not guarantee physical contiguity or a device-visible contiguous address range.

slides.title: Count a partial last page without overflowing first
keyPoints: Floor division alone misses a partial page
Use quotient plus a nonzero-remainder test
Zero bytes require zero pages in this model
slides.narration: The model uses eight-byte pages and sizes zero, one, eight, and nine. Dividing by eight alone gives zero, zero, one, and one, which undercounts one byte and nine bytes. The corrected calculation adds one when a remainder exists, giving zero, one, one, and two. The plus-one is applied to the quotient rather than forming size plus seven first. That avoids overflow in a common rounding-up expression for very large sizes. This example counts storage for a region beginning at a page boundary; an unaligned start would also affect the number of pages touched. State that assumption before applying the formula to an arbitrary pointer range.

slides.title: Where the simple approach fails
keyPoints: Multiplying the virtual page number by the page size reconstructs a virtual address, not the translated physical address.

A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Use pages[page] when only looking up a map. That operation can insert a default entry and make an unmapped page appear to map to frame zero.
The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Use find for a read-only lookup and handle end explicitly. Keep absence distinct from a valid mapping to frame zero.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A page is a fixed-size unit in the virtual address space.
A mapping associates a virtual page with backing storage and permissions.
Pages should not be confused with C objects: a page can contain many objects, part of one object, or bytes that no live language object currently occupies.
A large allocation can span many pages.
slides.narration:
A page is a fixed-size unit in the virtual address space. A mapping associates a virtual page with backing storage and permissions. Pages should not be confused with C objects: a page can contain many objects, part of one object, or bytes that no live language object currently occupies. A large allocation can span many pages. Crossing its internal page boundaries is valid when the allocation and mappings permit it. Conversely, staying within one page does not prove an array index is valid. Object-level bounds and page-level mapping boundaries solve different problems.

In plain English: The program uses a map of memory addresses. The operating system translates that map to where the data is actually stored.

slides.title: Page offset
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: For a page size of 2^p bytes, the low p address bits form the page offset.
With 4096-byte pages, p = 12 .
The offset is address mod 4096 , or equivalently address & 0xFFF for the nonnegative integer model.
Translation preserves these low bits when mapping a page to an equal-sized frame.
slides.narration:
For a page size of 2^p bytes, the low p address bits form the page offset. With 4096-byte pages, p = 12 . The offset is address mod 4096 , or equivalently address & 0xFFF for the nonnegative integer model. Translation preserves these low bits when mapping a page to an equal-sized frame. Only the page-number portion changes. This separation makes the final physical-address calculation straightforward and explains why correctly aligned page bases have zeroes in the offset positions.

In plain English: The program uses a map of memory addresses. The operating system translates that map to where the data is actually stored.

keyPoints: With 4 KiB pages, the page offset is 12 bits because 4096 = 2^12 .

Translation replaces the virtual page number with a physical frame number while preserving the offset.

With 4 KiB pages, the page offset is 12 bits because 4096 = 2^12 . For virtual address 0x12345 , the offset is 0x345 and the virtual page number is 0x12 . Translation replaces the virtual page number with a physical frame number while preserving the offset.

In plain English: Think of an address written on a note: the note can tell you where to look, but it does not prove the thing is still there or that you are allowed to use it.

slides.title: The low bits describe the byte within the page
keyPoints: 4096 bytes equals two to the twelfth power
Twelve low bits form the offset
Bit masks depend on a power-of-two assumption
slides.narration: For four-kibibyte pages, the offset ranges from zero through four thousand ninety-five. Twelve bits can represent exactly that many choices. In an unsigned integer model, address modulo four thousand ninety-six agrees with masking by hexadecimal FFF, and dividing agrees with shifting right twelve bits. These equivalences depend on the stated power-of-two page size. A generic arithmetic model with a positive size of ten would still support division and remainder, but the same mask would be wrong. In source maintenance, keep geometry in one named place and test both the final byte of a page and the first byte of the next page.
actions: Predict the result and name the mapping or invariant that supports it before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: What are the page number and offset of address 4096 with 4096-byte pages?
question.answer: Page one and offset zero; this is the first byte of the next page.

slides.title: Page size is a policy tradeoff, not a free upgrade
keyPoints: Larger pages cover more bytes per translation
Sparse use can waste backing storage
Runtime assumptions must match the platform
slides.narration: A translation entry covers more bytes when the page size grows. That can reduce translation pressure for a large densely used region. But a larger page can also bring in or reserve storage that a sparse workload barely touches. Allocation, migration, and protection granularity change too. The chapter uses four-kibibyte pages for calculation, not as a universal constant for every machine and mapping. If a program needs the operating system’s actual page size, obtain it through the relevant platform interface. A classroom bit diagram is useful only when its page size and address width are written beside it.
actions: Predict the result and name the mapping or invariant that supports it before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: Why might huge pages be a poor fit for many tiny sparsely touched regions?
question.answer: Their larger allocation and mapping granularity can waste storage or complicate management despite increased translation coverage.

slides.title: A missing mapping is a distinct result
keyPoints: Lookup may find no page entry
Do not treat frame zero as missing
An optional separates absence from a valid address
slides.narration: Frame zero is a legitimate number in a simplified translation model. If zero is also used as a lookup-failed marker, a valid mapping can be mistaken for failure. The source lab uses optional to distinguish no translation from a translated numeric address. A caller tests presence before dereferencing the optional. This is ordinary model-level error reporting, not a simulated hardware fault handler. A real operating system may recover a legitimate absent mapping through demand paging or reject an invalid request. The translation helper intentionally does less: it returns no value when its table cannot supply a safe result.

slides.title: Check multiplication before constructing an address
keyPoints: Frame × size + offset must fit the result type
Use maximum minus offset before division
Type correctness does not prove arithmetic range
slides.narration: An unsigned type has a largest representable value. Multiplying an arbitrary frame number by page size can wrap, producing a small number that looks like a valid address. The lab checks whether frame exceeds maximum minus offset, divided by page size, before performing the multiplication. Its page size is nonzero and the offset is bounded, so the guard itself is meaningful. This is a proof obligation in the integer model, not a claim that arbitrary frame numbers are legal hardware mappings. A compiler can accept overflowing unsigned arithmetic because wraparound is defined; tests still need to reject a wrapped result when it violates the translation contract.

slides.narration: Consider copying twelve bytes beginning four bytes before a page boundary. The first four bytes use one translation; the remaining eight use another. A successful first-byte check proves neither that the second page exists nor that the whole destination object has enough space. A robust range operation checks its length arithmetic, object bounds, and relevant mapping permissions at the correct layer. In normal application code, prefer established buffer APIs and lengths rather than inventing a userspace page-permission check as a substitute for object safety. Our tiny span trace is useful because it makes the otherwise hidden boundary crossing explicit.
